Sanitize the input text as done aboveParse the text into sentencesDetermine the words in the last sentence of the input text. Use upto the last 4 words from the input text.The word predictions are done starting from the ngram table containing the longest sequence of words, provided the input text contains atleast n-1 words. So, if the last 4 words from the input text match the first 4 words in the pentagram table, then the fifth word is chosen, that has the highest frequency of occurance after those 4 words. If more than one word prediction is desired, then the fifth words with the next highest frequency of occurance are also chosen.If no matches or fewer than desired number of matches are found in the pentagram table, then the algorithm backoffs to the quadrigram table using the last 3 words typed, then to the trigram table using the last 2 words typed, then to the bigram table using the last word typed and finally to the unigram table, until the desired number of word predictions are returned.Let’s see how this works concretely with some test cases:
Test CasesThe first test is to confirm whether the word predictions from the unigram table, match with what we expect.The top 10 unigram table contains 3 words beginning with the letter ‘t’ - the(1), to(4), that(10). And sure enough, this is what we get from our prediction function.
predictNextWords("t")[1] "Predictions from 1grams: the,to,that,this,thou"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: the,to,that"From the bigram table, we could see that i am, i have and i will are among the top 10. So, the next test is to confirm these.
predictNextWords("i ")[1] "Predictions from 2grams: am,have,will,do,would"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: am,have,will"Narrowing down to words that begin with letter ‘h’ gives us:
predictNextWords("i h")[1] "Predictions from 2grams: have,had,hope,hear,heard"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: have,had,hope"Let’s predict some trigrams. i am not and i am a are among the top 10 trigrams, so that’s what we expect to see.
predictNextWords("i am ")[1] "Predictions from 3grams: not,a,sure,glad,the"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: not,a,sure"Now let’s examine the UNK feature. We know that the UNK of is number 5 most common sequence in the trigram table so we should expect to see ‘of’ as the first prediction if the input text has an unknown word after ‘the’. So let’s input some gibberish after ‘the’ to make sure this word doesn’t exist in our vocabulary:
predictNextWords("the sjdhsbhbfh ")[1] "Predictions from 3grams: of,and,in,that,the"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: of,and,in"Now that the known test cases are working well, let’s see the backoff algorithm in action:
predictNextWords("to be or not ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: to"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: to"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: to,at,i,allow'd,arriv'd"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: to,at,i"predictNextWords("to be or not to ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: be"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: be,crack"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: be,crack,the,have,me,do"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: be,crack,the"predictNextWords("be or not to ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: be"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: be,crack"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: be,crack,the,have,me,do"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: be,crack,the"predictNextWords("to be or not to be ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: that"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: that,found,gone,endur'd,endured,seen"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: that,found,gone"predictNextWords("to be or not to be, that ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: is"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: is,which"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: is,which,you,he,i,thou,can"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: is,which,you"predictNextWords("to be or not to be, that is ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: the"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: the"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: the,not,my,to,a"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: the,not,my"predictNextWords("to be or not to be, that is the ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: question"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: question,very,way,humour,best,brief"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: question,very,way"predictNextWords("be that is the ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: question"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: question,very,way,humour,best,brief"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: question,very,way"Using one of the most well known speeches from Hamlet, we can see that the algorithm gets the first word prediction from the pentagram table. But since we are looking for the next 3 words, the algorithm backoffs to predictions from quadrigram and trigram tables, until it has atleast 3 words. In this case, the pentagram table gives us the best match that we are looking for. We can also observe that once we have atleast 4 words in our input text, the words prior to those do not matter for the next word predictions.
Let’s see another example:
predictNextWords("What a lovely day ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: "[1] "Predictions from 4grams: "[1] "Predictions from 3grams: "[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"predictNextWords("a lovely day ")[1] "Predictions from 4grams: "[1] "Predictions from 3grams: "[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"predictNextWords("lovely day ")[1] "Predictions from 3grams: "[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"predictNextWords("day ")[1] "Predictions from 2grams: and,to,is,of,i"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: and,to,is"Here we see that even though there are enough words to start matching from the higher ngram tables, the matches are gotten only from the bigram table using ‘day’ as the first word.
Another one:
predictNextWords("Beware the ides of ")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 2grams: march,the,my,his,a,this"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: march,the,my"predictNextWords("Beware the ides of mar")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 2grams: march,marriage,marcius,marcus,mars"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: march,marriage,marcius"predictNextWords("Beware the ides of march")[1] "Predictions from 5grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 4grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 3grams: march"[1] "Predictions from 2grams: march,marching"[1] "Predictions from 1grams: march,marching,march'd,marches,marchioness"[1] "Top 3 Final Predictions: march,marching,march'd"Shiny AppFinally, here’s a Shiny app that demos this predictive typing model.
The R markdown file for this post is available here.
summary: Everyone using a smartphone or a mobile device has used an onscreen smart keyboard that tries to predict the next set of words that the user might want to type. Typically, upto 3 words are predicted, which are displayed in a row at the top of the keyboard. Given that typing on a glass pane without tactile feedback, could be very frustrating at times, the smart keyboard goes a long way in alleviating these issues.
title: Building a Predictive Typing Model

Who’re the best batsmen in cricket today? Is there a way to define a set of objective criteria that provides an unbiased conclusion? In my last post, I selected a list of top batsmen in the history of cricket, by simply filtering all batsmen who have had a career batting average of 50 or more in any format. Prior to that I eliminated newcomers, specialist bowlers and unsuccessful players by another set of filters.
I got a list of 42 batsmen who have consistently performed well throughout their career. Now the question is how could we select the best of the best who have had the most well-rounded performances. A post on fivethirtyeight has been a strong inspiration to arrive at the answers below.
Best batsmen at presentTo select current best batsmen we filter the list of top batsmen to include only the batsmen who are actively playing in all the 3 formats of the game.
This leaves us with only 6 batsmen who are currently playing in all the formats. They are AB de Villiers, HM Amla, JE Root, KS Williamson, SPD Smith, V Kohli. No surprises there as these batsmen are widely considered to be the best among the active players today. But instead of subjectively handpicking them, we arrived at this conclusion by applying some reasonable filters.
But how well-rounded are these players? To determine this I’ve defined the following criteria and metrics:
CriteriaMetricLabelConsistency of scoring runsCareer batting averageSCORING CONSISTENCYAbility to score quicklyStrike RateSTRIKE RATEAbility to score big (number of 100s + number of 50s scored)Big scores per inningsBIG SCORING RATEOverall contribution to the matches playedTeam Win-Loss RatioWIN RATIODirect contribution to matches wonBatting average in winning matchesWIN CONTRIBUTIONEvery metric defined here is a ratio instead of an absolute number. So it is useful to evaluate relative ability.
Among the 42 top batsmen selected before, I calculate percentile scores of these metrics for each batsman grouped by the format of the game. This means we have a score ranging from 0-100 for each metric, where each batsman in the list has been scored relative to the best batsman in each criteria.
Let’s see the percentile scores for the 6 champion batsmen in our final list.
Percentile ScoresFormatCountryPlayerPercAveragePercStrikeRatePercInningsPerBigScorePercWinRatioPercAverageInWins1TestsSouth AfricaAB de Villiers20572761472ODIsSouth AfricaAB de Villiers1001008672933T20IsSouth AfricaAB de Villiers36733188324TestsSouth AfricaHM Amla8402274305ODIsSouth AfricaHM Amla83909379836T20IsSouth AfricaHM Amla59626244507TestsEnglandJE Root54708120868ODIsEnglandJE Root76738915869T20IsEnglandJE Root896770327510TestsNew ZealandKS Williamson324476157611ODIsNew ZealandKS Williamson696982297512T20IsNew ZealandKS Williamson715077756313TestsAustraliaSPD Smith988386379114ODIsAustraliaSPD Smith568352755815T20IsAustraliaSPD Smith18458571916TestsIndiaV Kohli10798641817ODIsIndiaV Kohli949797659718T20IsIndiaV Kohli10084939494Here we can see how each champion scored relative to the rest of the elite group. AB de Villiers has the best career batting average and strike rate in ODIs so he gets a score of 100 in SCORING CONSISTENCY & STRIKE RATE. All other batsmen are scored relative to AB in these 2 criteria. With his astounding batting average of 99.94 in Tests, Sir Don Bradman gets a score of 100 in SCORING CONSISTENCY in Tests. And being at number 5 in all time highest batting averages in Tests, Steve Smith gets a high score of 91 in this criteria, relative to Sir Don.
This is all well and good, but how do we see the forest from trees? It is very difficult to make sense of high dimensional data in a table or in a single bar plot. This is where the visualization technique shown in the fivethirtyeight article shines. We build a wagon wheel with segments denoting each metric and within each segment, the data is binned by quartiles.
Here’s how a wagon wheel would look like for each batsman. Each segment would be filled depending upon the percentile score in each criteria.
So let’s see how the wagon wheels of our champions look like:
We see that Steve Smith is the most well-rounded batsman in Tests. His WIN RATIO is lacking relative to the illustrious company he’s in, but overall his performance in Tests is phenomenal. Joe Root comes second but others have a bit more catching up to do.
In One Day Internationals, Hashim Amla dominates in all spheres with AB de Villiers and Virat Kohli not far behind. Joe Root seems to contribute in most matches won by England but it appears the English team loses a fair bit in ODIs. Hence the WIN RATIO of Root is a bit lacking.
Virat Kohli is the undisputed king in the T20 Internationals format with Kane Williamson in second place. Steve Smith’s performance so far leaves much to be desired in this format.
The beauty of this visualization technique is that several dimensions in the data are compressed in a single facetted plot, in a visually appealing way. A glance at the plot reveals the relative best, both overall and in each metric.

In a previous post, I used data from Statsguru and looked at a brief history of cricket with respect to debut years and career spans of players. In this post, I use detailed player statistics from the same dataset to select top batsmen who have played this game.
Distribution of matches played by all playersLet’s take a look at the summary statistics of number of matches played by all players in each format of the game.
Number of matches played by all players in each formatFormat: TestsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 1.00 2.00 7.00 17.27 21.00 200.00 --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Format: ODIsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 1.00 4.00 16.00 42.56 53.00 463.00 --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Format: T20IsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 1.0 2.0 7.0 13.9 18.5 98.0 The distribution appears to be heavily skewed towards the right. In simple terms, there are a handful of players who go on to play 100+ Tests and 200+ ODIs. A majority of the players have played very few matches. The mean and median are hardly indicative of players who established themselves in their teams.
Distribution of innings to matches played by all playersA cricket team has 11 players, out of which 5 or 6 are specialist batsmen, 1 or 2 are all-rounders (could bat and bowl well) and the rest are specialist bowlers. The wicketkeeper also has to be a good batsman. The batsmen play up in the order in a match and get to bat before the bowlers do.
Here I will introduce another measure to distinguish batsmen from bowlers - ratio of innings played relative to number of matches played. In many matches a bowler doesn’t get a chance to bat, unless the top order batsmen and all-rounders fail, i.e. are out. Hence the ratio of innings to matches of specialist bowlers will be low.
Here are the summary statistics of this ratio. The ratio is greater than 1 in Tests because each player could play upto 2 innings. The peaks in each plot are indicative of batsmen who have batted in the top 3 and have gotten a chance to bat in nearly every innings of every match they played.
Ratio of innings to matches of all players in each formatFormat: TestsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. NAs 0.250 1.429 1.667 1.623 1.923 2.000 19 --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Format: ODIsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. NAs 0.1250 0.5714 0.8421 0.7670 1.0000 1.0000 62 --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Format: T20IsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. NAs 0.05556 0.50000 0.85714 0.73084 1.00000 1.00000 73 Distinguish batsmen from bowlersTo identify true batsmen in the dataset, I use 2 filters:
Number of matches played should be above the 75th percentileRatio of innings to matches played should be above the 25th percentileThe first filter eliminates newcomers and players who have had very short-lived careers. The second filter eliminates specialist bowlers from the dataset.
Let’s take a look at the distribution of these metrics for these batsmen. These numbers appear more reasonable.
Career averages of batsmenLet’s take a look at the career batting averages of batsmen in each format. We see a few low averaging players left in the dataset who are potentially specialist bowlers. But without resorting to hand-picking, the two empirical filters chosen earlier did a good job of eliminating specialist bowlers from the dataset.
Career batting averages of batsmen in each formatFormat: TestsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 4.84 24.84 33.59 33.11 42.13 99.94 --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Format: ODIsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 6.63 23.11 29.71 29.55 35.88 55.03 --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Format: T20IsMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 4.10 18.15 21.91 23.27 28.44 53.40 Top batsmenThe hallmark of a top batsman is consistency in scoring runs. From the distribution of career averages, it could be seen that very few batsmen have managed to score at an average of 50 or more runs in their career. So keeping things simple, this would be my sole criteria for selecting top batsmen amongst the rest. All batsmen who have averaged 50 or more in any format would be included in my list of top batsmen.
This gives us a unique list of 42 elite batsmen who are legendary in their achievements.
Let’s take a look how they compare by various stats.
Career SpanThe career span of these elite batsmen is plotted in the order in which they debuted in their international career. Career spans of batsmen who are still actively playing in any format are labeled with blue color.
Summary of career spans in years of top batsmenMin. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 5.00 11.00 16.00 14.71 18.75 24.00 Sachin Tendulkar and George Headley have had the longest career spans of 24 years each. But the international career of Headley along with that of almost all of the early era greats were interrupted by world wars. So even though they resumed their careers after the end of the wars, they were able to play relatively few matches (more on this below).
Graeme Pollock has had the shortest career of 7 years amongst all retired players. Being a South African, his career was cut short when ICC suspended South Africa from competing internationally in 1970 because of apartheid.
Number of matches playedAmong the many records in Tendulkar’s name, the number of Tests and ODIs played are at the forefront. He played a single T20I, because he, Dravid and other senior members of the then Indian team used to withdraw their names for team selection in T20Is. His records of playing in 200 Tests and 463 ODIs are a testament to his brilliance, his passion for the game and his fitness over the years. Among the active players only AB de Villiers and Hashim Amla are at the halfway mark relatively to Tendulkar’s mark in Tests. But both AB and Amla are already well into their prime years. Younis Khan is on the verge of riding into the sunset. The rest of the pack including Virat Kohli, Kane Williamson, Steve Smith have a looong way to catch up.
It could be observed how few matches did the early era greats play relatively. Not only were few teams competing at the time, but also interruptions by world wars.
Michael Bevan established himself as an ODI specialist and played only 18 tests. Cheteshwar Pujara appears to have barely made the cutoffs for this list. He is a Tests specialist.
Career runs scoredOnce again Tendulkar’s records here are at the top. It is highly unlikely that any other batsman could ever come close in the next 5-10 years.
Career batting averagesFirst and foremost is Sir Don Bradman’s career batting average record of 99.94 in Tests. He is widely regarded to be the greatest batsman of all time. This is one record that’s impossible to beat. The second batsman on this list is Graeme Pollock at 60.97. Steve Smith is the only active batsman who is anywhere close to second, a phenomenal achievement in its own right.
Secondly, it becomes clear why each batsman was selected for this list, a batting average of 50 or more in any single format. Though most batsmen have a Tests average above 50, Jonathan Trott, MS Dhoni and Michael Bevan made it by virtue of their superlative averages in the ODIs.
Virat Kohli is the only batsman who has averaged above 50 in all the 3 formats.
Hundreds scored in careerOnce again Tendulkar leads in the standings with 51 hundreds in Tests and 49 hundreds in ODIs. Sir Don’s record Test average of 99.94, Tendulkar’s records of number of matches played, runs scored and hundreds scored in career are some of the records that are going to be next to impossible to beat.
Surprisingly none of the batsmen on this list have scored a hundred in T20Is. There are a few other batsmen who have scored hundreds in T20Is but none of them were consistent enough to make it to this list.
Highest scores in an inningsHere we see the great Brian Lara at the top of the Tests table with a highest score of 400 not out. I remember Sir Garfield Sobers’ score of 365 not out was one of the longest standing records in Test cricket until Lara surpassed it. Only Matthew Hayden was able to come any closer to Lara.
In ODIs, it was apt that the champion, Sachin Tendulkar was the first one to score a double hundred. A few other batsmen have scored 200+ scores in ODIs since, but none have had the consistency that Tendulkar had.
In T20Is, as mentioned above none of these batsman scored a hundred. Though a few have come close. I expect some of the active players to reach this milestone in the near future.

Since early childhood, I have been a big fan of cricket. Some of my earliest childhood memories are watching the game along with my loved ones in India. As much as I can recall, the first series I saw was between India and the West Indies during the early 80s, on a black and white TV set. Watching Sunil Gavaskar play the fearsome West Indian fast bowlers with aplomb, made me his fan…until a kid named Sachin Tendulkar arrived in 1989.
As the saying goes…In India, cricket is religion and Tendulkar is God! Even after his retirement in 2013, Tendulkar is still the most loved sportsperson or celebrity in India. A billion people passionately follow the game and voice their opinion on matters of team selection, players’ performances, umpiring…you name it. Armchair analysts abound, especially if the Indian cricket team loses a consequential match or a series.
I was excited to find that detailed records and stats on all cricket players were available on Statsguru. The database covers all formats of the game:
Tests - Test matches (80 overs a day, each team playing upto 2 innings in 5 days)ODIs - One-Day Internationals (50 overs an innings)T20Is - Twenty20 Internationals (20 overs an innings)In this post, I’ve tried to examine a brief history of the game using the debut years and career spans of players.
Here’s a sample of batting data:
Batting records of players who have represented Australia in ODIsPlayerSpanMatInnsNORunsHSAveBFSR1005001RT Ponting1995-2012374364391358916441.811694480.192982202AC Gilchrist1996-200828627811959517235.93990296.891655193ME Waugh1988-200224423620850017339.351105376.91850164MJ Clarke2003-201524522344798113044.581010478.98858105SR Waugh1986-2002325288587569120*32.90997175.91345156MG Bevan1994-2004232196676912108*53.58932074.166465Here’s a sample of bowling data:

I downloaded batting and bowling data for all of these 10 teams in all 3 formats. The dataset is rich with features and appears to cover the entire history of international cricket.
Major props to the folks at Statsguru for maintaining a clean dataset. Both batting and bowling datasets have the same number of players, as should be the case. So there wasn’t much data wrangling needed.
Here are what the abbreviations mean:
TermDescriptionSpanSeparate into debut year and last year of careerMatMatches played in careerInnsInnings played in careerNONumber of times not out in careerHSHighest batting score in careerAveCareer Average, batting: Runs/(Innings - NotOuts), bowling: Runs/WicketsBFBalls FacedSRStrike Rate, batting: Runs/Balls Faced, bowling: Balls/WicketsBBIBest bowling performance in an inningsBallsNumber of balls bowled in careerWktsNumber of wickets in careerEconBowling economy rate: Runs per over (Overs bowled = Balls bowled/6)100Number of hundreds scored in career50Number of fifties scored in career4Number of times the bowler took 4 wickets in an innings5Number of times the bowler took 5 or more wickets in an inningsWhen did each country first play internationally?From the earliest debut years of players, it could be seen when each format was started and when each country started playing in a format. Australia and England have been the pioneering nations in each format. The earliest Tests were played between Australia and England in 1877. South Africa joined the fray in 1889. For the next 40 years, these were the only 3 international teams, until West Indies, India and New Zealand started playing in quick succession. In 1970 South Africa was suspended from playing international cricket by the ICC because of prevailing apartheid in the nation. As a result, the international career of some very promising South Africans like Graeme Pollock and Barry Richards ended abruptly. Later on some other players emigrated to England and Australia to get a chance to play internationally. This ban was lifted by the ICC in 1991. The newly formed South African team under Clive Rice was given a warm welcome in India, when they visited to play ODIs. South Africa resumed playing tests in 1992.
Sri Lanka, Zimbabwe and Bangladesh were Associate members with ODI status before they were elected as full members to be eligible to play Tests.
Number of players who have represented their country internationallyEven though Australia and England started playing Tests together in 1877, there have been far more players representing the England team in Tests, when looking at the entire history. This suggests a lot more turnover in the English team.
Number of players who debuted internationally by yearThis plot shows the number of distinct players debuting each year. So, for instance, if a player debuted in Tests, ODIs and T20Is team in the same year, then that is counted as 1. Few things could be noted here:
The gaps in Australia, England and India facets show the years interrupted by the 2 world wars.As noted earlier, there’s a big gap in the South Africa facet, when the country was suspended from 1970-1991.The gaps in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Zimbabwe are because each country was an associate member of the ICC and was only competing in ICC ODI tournaments until the country got its full member status.There’s been a steady increase in the number of players debuting in Australia, England, India, Pakistan and West Indies, in the last decade or so. This suggests a trend of having specialist players in the team for each format. Top teams like Australia, England and India have adopted this trend. Some players are selected as Test match specialists, while the others are selected to only play in ODIs and T20Is.Career spans of playersTo examine the career spans of players, I filtered the dataset to only keep the players who haven’t been active in 2016-2017. Then I eliminated quick failures whose career didn’t last for more than 2 years. This meant the players left in the dataset were given enough opportunities to succeed at the international level. Then I examined the median career span by debut year.
It appears a median player used to play between 6 to 10 years before retiring. Although there was more dispersion in Tests, it was clearly the norm in ODIs. 1908 was an extreme outlier year in Tests because only 1 player qualified the inclusion criteria. This was Sir Jack Hobbs of England, an early master of the game who played for 23 years. 1909 was another extreme outlier year where only 3 players were included. These were the legends Warren Bardsley of Australia (18 years), Frank Woolley of England (26 years) and Bill Whitty of Australia (4 years).
An outlier in the ODIs plot corresponds to the year 1989. This was the year when some modern day legends made their debut. Most notably Sachin Tendulkar from India who played for 24 years. Saeed Anwar, Waqar Younis & Mushtaq Ahmed from Pakistan who each played for 15 years and Sanath Jayasuriya from Sri Lanka who played for 23 years. Alec Stewart and Nasser Hussain from England also debuted in 1989. They had checkered records in ODIs but overall their careers lasted for 15 years.
An astonishing trend appears to have started with the players debuting after the early 90s. Career spans of players peaked with those debuting during early 90s. Since then the median career span started dropping year by year. This could be seen across all formats. Although the median career span would change for more recent years as active players playing from early 2000s retire in future, nevertheless this trend is persistent from early 90s.
Matches played by debut yearsThe same downwards trends from early 90s could also be observed in the median number of matches played by debut year. This isn’t surprising as the number of matches played is directly correlated with career span. An upward trend from early 30s could be observed in Test matches played. This is explained by the addition of West Indies, New Zealand and India as full members of the ICC from late 20s. Every international player started playing more matches as the number of competing teams doubled to 6.
A big upward trend could be seen in ODIs from its inception. Until the beginning of ODIs, cricket was only played in Tests format that was characteristically very laid back. Both teams got a chance to bat upto 2 innings alternately over 5 days. More often than not the matches would end in a draw with no win/loss result. The introduction of 60 overs a side ODIs (later reduced to 50 overs a side) format was to be played in a single day. The team batting first would set a target score. Then the team batting second would chase this target. This ensured guaranteed results although there have been few occasions where the ODIs have resulted in ties at the same score. Naturally this format was more palatable to spectators and TV audiences that contributed to a rapid growth in its popularity. The ODIs format is still the most popular format till date.
In the next couple of posts I will analyze batting performances.

As much as I can recall, the first series I saw was between India and the West Indies during the early 80s, on a black and white TV set. Watching Sunil Gavaskar play the fearsome West Indian fast bowlers with aplomb, made me his fan…until a kid named Sachin Tendulkar arrived in 1989.

In a previous post in this series, we explored the Ames Housing dataset.
In this post, we build linear and non-linear models, and we find out how well they predict the SalePrice of properties. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. A linear model adds up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that it learns from the data. A non-linear model can also learn curved relationships.
Evaluation CriteriaTo measure how good a model is, we use the root mean squared error (RMSE) between the log of the predicted price and the log of the actual SalePrice. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, so a lower RMSE is better. We use the log of the prices so that an error of 10% counts the same for an expensive house and for a cheap house.
Steps for Building ModelsEach model has settings that it cannot learn from the data. We must choose them before training. These settings are called hyperparameters. To choose the best hyperparameters, we use K-fold cross validation, as described in the steps below:
Remove features that repeat the information of other features, and change ordinal features into scores.Split the training data into K parts (folds). Each time, the model learns from all the folds except one (the training part), and we check its predictions on the remaining fold (the validation part). We split the data in a way that keeps a similar mix of prices in each fold (stratified sampling).Choose the linear and non-linear models to use.For each model, make a set (a grid) of hyperparameter combinations that covers the possible values evenly (a space-filling grid).For each combination, train the model on the training part and make predictions on the validation part. Repeat this for all the folds.Calculate the RMSE, and choose the combination with the lowest RMSE.Train each model again, with its best combination, on the complete training set.Calculate the RMSE of each final model on the testing set, which has properties that the models have not seen.Choose the model with the lowest RMSE.Removing Collinear PredictorsMany features in this dataset describe the same thing in different ways. Also, some of the features that we created in the previous post repeat others. A model cannot use categories directly, so each category becomes a separate feature with the values 0 and 1 (a dummy variable). After this change, some features are exact combinations of other features (we call them collinear). A linear model cannot separate the effects of collinear features. So its coefficients become unreliable, or it cannot calculate them at all, and lm (the basic linear model in R) gives a warning about a “rank-deficient fit”. Models that use decision trees are not affected by repeated information. But if we remove it, the linear models work correctly and all the models are simpler.
The association matrix in the previous post showed which features repeat each other. We drop these features, because other features already give their information:
HasGarage, HasFireplace and HasMasVnr are the same as, or almost the same as, the None category of GarageType, FireplaceQu and MasVnrType.MSSubClass combines the type and the style of a building. BldgType and HouseStyle already give this information. Its duplex category is identical to the duplex category of BldgType.TotalBath is exactly FullBath + 0.5 * HalfBath + BsmtBath. We drop HalfBath, not TotalBath. So we keep the total, which is one of the most important features for the decision tree models. And we lose no information, because we can calculate HalfBath from the other three features.Encoding Ordinal FeaturesThe categories of features such as OverallQual or KitchenQual have a natural order. These are ordinal features. By default, step_dummy() changes an ordinal feature into several features called polynomial contrasts. It makes one new feature for each category except one, and these features describe straight, curved and more complex trends across the grades. But some grades are very rare. For example, only one property has an OverallCond of 1. So a rare grade can be missing from a fold. Then some of these new features become collinear in that fold.
Instead, we change each ordinal feature into one whole number (a score) that follows the order of its categories: 1, 2, 3 and so on. This assumes that the steps between the grades are equal. First, we drop the categories that no property has, such as a Poor exterior quality, so that the scores have no gaps. Here are the results of a linear model with each method, on the same folds:

The simpler method works better on new data, because the model does not have to learn a separate effect for each rare grade.Finally, step_lincomb() checks whether any features are still exact combinations of other features. This could happen because properties without a basement or a garage have the None category in every basement or garage feature. With scores, it finds no such features.

Regularization adds a penalty for large coefficients. This makes the model keep only the effects that the data clearly supports. glmnet combines two types of regularization: LASSO (L1), which can reduce the coefficient of a feature to exactly 0, and Ridge (L2), which makes all the coefficients smaller. Appendix: Tuning CodeThis is the code that tunes the models. It takes several minutes, so it does not run each time we build this page. Instead, the page saves the results in the file Ames_Tuning.Rda, together with a fingerprint (a hash) of the inputs of the tuning. The inputs are the clean data from the previous post and the tuning code itself, which also sets the hyperparameter grids. When we build the page again, it calculates the fingerprint again:
If the fingerprint is the same, the page loads the saved results in a few seconds.If the data, a hyperparameter or any other part of the tuning code has changed, the page tunes the models again and saves the new results.Changes to the comments or the spacing of the code do not count as changes. To tune the models again without any change, delete Ames_Tuning.Rda.
These are the tuning steps:
# Why the tuning code is built the way it is (speed):# The dataset is small (1,460 rows x ~150 predictors after encoding), so run time is driven by the# number of model fits (5 models x 25 grid points x 5 folds) and by how expensive each fit is, not by data size.# The earlier version took ~35 minutes; this version takes ~11 minutes with 6 workers, tuning the same models and# hyperparameters (with randomForest replaced by the equivalent ranger engine). The changes:# 1. tune_grid() parallelises over every fold x grid-point combination ("everything"), instead of a manual# for-loop over grid points that only ran the 5 folds in parallel and left the remaining cores idle.# 2. Random forest uses only the `ranger` engine with 500 trees. The `randomForest` package was tuned in addition# to ranger and gave the same cross-validated RMSE (0.135 vs 0.134). On one fold with mtry = 84, min_n = 2:# randomForest, 1,000 trees: 46.9s, RMSE 0.1305# ranger, 1,000 trees: 15.1s, RMSE 0.1303# ranger, 500 trees: 7.2s, RMSE 0.1293# Random forest error levels off well before 500 trees on data of this size, so 1,000 trees only doubled the cost.# 3. xgboost searches a sensible learning-rate range, instead of spending much of the grid on learning rates as# small as 1e-10 that cannot converge in 1,000 rounds (see get_model_param_grid). Early stopping was tried and# rejected; see the note in get_model_spec.# 4. The number of parallel workers is capped by available RAM as well as CPU cores (see "Parallel backend").## Unrelated to speed: the earlier version used Id as a predictor. It is now excluded (see get_workflow).# It also had 21 predictors that were exact linear combinations of others, which lm reported as a rank-deficient# fit. They are now removed (see "Collinear predictors" and get_preprocessing_recipe), leaving a full-rank design.# Ordered factors are encoded as integer scores instead of polynomial contrasts (see get_preprocessing_recipe).# load the clean dataset from Part 1 (ames_data_file is set in the "tuning_cache" chunk)load(ames_data_file)# Collinear predictors######################################################################################################################################################### With the earlier set of features, 21 of the ~250 predictors were exact linear combinations of others (the design# matrix had rank 229 of 250), so lm could not estimate them and warned of a rank-deficient fit. Tree models are not# affected by duplicated information, but linear models are: the coefficients of collinear predictors are unstable.# These features are dropped because other features already carry their information (see the association matrix# in Part 1):# HasGarage, HasFireplace, HasMasVnr: the same as the "None" category of GarageType, FireplaceQu and MasVnrType.# MSSubClass: combines the building type and style, already in BldgType and HouseStyle (bias-corrected Cramer's V# of 0.89 and 0.83). Its "duplex" category is identical to BldgType's.# HalfBath: TotalBath = FullBath + 0.5 * HalfBath + BsmtBath exactly. Dropping HalfBath rather than TotalBath# keeps the total, one of the most important features for the tree models, and loses no information# because HalfBath can be recovered from the other three.vFeaturesCollinear <- c("HasGarage", "HasFireplace", "HasMasVnr", "MSSubClass", "HalfBath")# Categories that no property has (e.g. a Poor exterior quality) are dropped too, so that the scores of ordered factors# are consecutive (see get_preprocessing_recipe).dfClean <- dfClean %>%select(-all_of(vFeaturesCollinear)) %>%mutate(across(where(is.factor), droplevels))# Determine skewed featuresvFeaturesSkew <- dfClean %>%select_if(is.numeric) %>%select_if(function(Z) abs(timeDate::skewness(Z, na.rm = T)) > 0.75) %>%colnames() %>%setdiff(c("Id","PropertyAge"))# Remove Outliers and split clean data######################################################################################################################################################### dfClean <- dfClean %>% dplyr::filter(!(Id %in% c(524, 1299))) # glmnet cv_rmse improves to 0.117 but test_rmse is 0.135dfTrain <- dfClean %>% filter(!(Id %in% vTestIDs))dfTest <- dfClean %>% filter(Id %in% vTestIDs)# Preprocessing Recipe######################################################################################################################################################### Ordered factors (quality and condition grades, etc.) are encoded as integer scores, one predictor per feature, in# the order of their categories. The alternative, step_dummy's polynomial contrasts, creates one predictor per category# but one. Grades that only a handful of properties have can then be missing from a cross validation fold, which makes# the highest-order contrasts collinear: with that encoding lm reported a rank-deficient fit in 4 of the 5 folds. Scores# assume the grades are equally spaced, which is a reasonable approximation for these grades, and they cut the# number of predictors from ~214 to ~151. dfEncodingComparison below compares the two encodings.## step_lincomb removes any remaining exact linear combinations among the predictors. These can arise because properties# without a basement or garage share the "None" category of every basement or garage feature. An intercept column is# added for the check, because such combinations can include a constant, and removed afterwards.get_preprocessing_recipe <- function(df, ordinalScores = TRUE) {preprocessing_recipe <- recipe(SalePrice ~ ., data = df) %>%update_role(Id, new_role = "ID") %>%step_mutate_at(one_of(vFeaturesSkew), -all_outcomes(), fn = ~ log(. + 1L))if(ordinalScores) {preprocessing_recipe <- preprocessing_recipe %>%step_ordinalscore(all_ordered_predictors())}preprocessing_recipe <- preprocessing_recipe %>%step_dummy(all_nominal()) %>%step_intercept() %>%step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%step_rm(any_of("intercept")) %>%step_log(all_outcomes()) %>%prep()return(preprocessing_recipe)}# The recipe is prepared on the training set only, and the same recipe is applied to the testing set (and to any new# data), so that both have exactly the same predictors.preprocessing_recipe <- get_preprocessing_recipe(dfTrain)# Preprocessed data for training modelsdfTrain_Proc <- preprocessing_recipe %>%bake(new_data = NULL) %>%rename(target = SalePrice) %>%select(target, everything())dfTest_Proc <- preprocessing_recipe %>%bake(new_data = dfTest) %>%rename(target = SalePrice) %>%select(target, everything())# Create cv folds########################################################################################################################################################get_cv_folds <- function(df, numFolds, strataVar, randomSeed, shuffleData) {# shuffle the rowsif(shuffleData) {set.seed(randomSeed)df <- df[sample(nrow(df)), ]}# split dataset into folds where each fold has the same distribution of targetlFolds <- df %>% vfold_cv(v = numFolds, strata = all_of(strataVar))return(lFolds)}# Parsnip Model Specification########################################################################################################################################################get_model_spec <- function(modelType) {model_spec <- switch(modelType,lm = linear_reg(mode = "regression") %>%set_engine("lm"),glmnet = linear_reg(mode = "regression", penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>%set_engine("glmnet"),# No early stopping. It was tried (stop after 50 rounds without improvement on a 10% validation split)# and roughly halved xgboost tuning time, but the final model was unstable: refitting the same best# parameters with different random validation splits stopped anywhere from 195 to 687 rounds, with test# RMSE between 0.133 and 0.151, versus 0.131 for a fixed 1,000 trees. With only ~146 validation rows the# stopping point is too noisy. The narrower learn_rate range already removes the wasted fits.# nthread = 1 because parallelism comes from running many fits at once (one per worker).xgboost = boost_tree(mode="regression", trees=1000, min_n=tune(), tree_depth=tune(), learn_rate=tune()) %>%set_engine("xgboost", objective = "reg:squarederror", nthread = 1),kernlab = svm_rbf(mode="regression", cost=tune(), rbf_sigma=tune(), margin=tune()) %>%set_engine("kernlab"),# ranger replaces the randomForest engine: same algorithm, ~3x faster implementation, and 500 trees# instead of 1,000 with no loss of accuracy (see the timings at the top of this code).# num.threads = 1 for the same reason as xgboost's nthread above.ranger = rand_forest(mode = "regression", trees = 500, mtry = tune(), min_n = tune()) %>%set_engine("ranger", num.threads = 1))return(model_spec)}# Parameter Grid Search########################################################################################################################################################get_model_param_grid <- function(df, modelType, numParams, randomSeed) {# mtry is finalized on the predictors only, so its upper bound is the number of predictors (excludes target and Id)dfPredictors <- df %>% select(-target, -Id)set.seed(randomSeed)param_spec <- switch(modelType,glmnet = parameters(penalty(), mixture()),kernlab = parameters(cost(), rbf_sigma(), svm_margin()),# learn_rate is on a log10 scale. The dials default (1e-10 to 1e-1) spends most of the grid on rates# so small that 1,000 trees barely move from the starting prediction: those fits take the full time# and are never competitive. 10^-2.5 to 10^-0.5 (~0.003 to ~0.3) covers the useful range; the best# rate found with the default range was ~0.07, comfortably inside it.xgboost = parameters(min_n(), tree_depth(), learn_rate(range = c(-2.5, -0.5))),ranger = parameters(min_n(), finalize(mtry(), dfPredictors)))dfParamGrid <- grid_space_filling(param_spec, size = numParams, type = "max_entropy")return(dfParamGrid)}# Workflow for a model######################################################################################################################################################### The data is already preprocessed, so the workflow only names the outcome and predictors.# Id is excluded from the predictors: it is a row identifier, and with training Ids 1-1460 and test Ids 1461-2919,# tree models would otherwise split on it and treat every test property as lying beyond the training range.get_workflow <- function(model_spec) {workflow() %>%add_variables(outcomes = target, predictors = -Id) %>%add_model(model_spec)}# Cross Validation Results######################################################################################################################################################### tune_grid() fits every grid point on every fold. With parallel_over = "everything", each (fold, grid point)# combination is a separate task, so all workers stay busy until the end of the run.# The mean RMSE across folds is the same metric as before (mean of the per-fold RMSE).cross_validate_model <- function(cv_folds, model_spec, param_grid) {tune_results <- get_workflow(model_spec) %>%tune_grid(resamples = cv_folds,grid = param_grid,metrics = metric_set(rmse),control = control_grid(parallel_over = "everything"))dfResults <- tune_results %>%collect_metrics() %>%select(all_of(names(param_grid)), mean_rmse = mean) %>%arrange(mean_rmse)return(dfResults)}# Fitted model with parameters######################################################################################################################################################### Returns a fitted workflow; predict() on it selects the predictor columns from new data, so Id can stay in the data.# The seed makes the final ranger and xgboost fits reproducible between runs.get_fitted_model <- function(df, model_spec, dfParams, randomSeed = 2300) {model_wf <- get_workflow(model_spec)if(!is.null(dfParams)) model_wf <- model_wf %>% finalize_workflow(dfParams)set.seed(randomSeed)fit(model_wf, data = df)}# Parallel backend######################################################################################################################################################### Each worker is a separate R session with tidymodels and the model packages loaded. In a full run with 5 workers,# no R process exceeded 0.6 GB and all R processes together (main session + workers) peaked at 3.2 GB. Budgeting# 0.75 GB per worker leaves headroom. Workers are capped at cores - 1 (to keep the machine responsive) and at what fits in 70% of the RAM# available when the run starts, so the run cannot push the machine into swapping even if other applications are open.gb_per_worker <- 0.75gb_available <- ps::ps_system_memory()$avail / 1024^3num_workers <- max(1, min(parallel::detectCores() - 1, floor(0.7 * gb_available / gb_per_worker)))message(sprintf("Using %d parallel workers (%.1f GB RAM available)", num_workers, gb_available))plan(multisession, workers = num_workers)# Create cross validation foldscv_folds <- get_cv_folds(dfTrain_Proc, numFolds = 5, strataVar = "target", randomSeed = 2300, shuffleData = T)# Compare the encodings of ordered factors with a linear model on the same folds (reported in the post)compare_encoding <- function(ordinalScores) {df <- get_preprocessing_recipe(dfTrain, ordinalScores) %>%bake(new_data = NULL) %>%rename(target = SalePrice) %>%select(target, everything())folds <- get_cv_folds(df, numFolds = 5, strataVar = "target", randomSeed = 2300, shuffleData = T)vAliased <- map_int(folds$splits, ~ sum(is.na(coef(lm(target ~ ., data = analysis(.x) %>% select(-Id))))))tibble(encoding = if(ordinalScores) "ordinal scores" else "polynomial contrasts",predictors = ncol(df) - 2,folds_rank_deficient = sum(vAliased > 0),lm_cv_rmse = suppressWarnings(get_workflow(get_model_spec("lm")) %>%fit_resamples(resamples = folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse)) %>%collect_metrics() %>%pull(mean)))}dfEncodingComparison <- bind_rows(compare_encoding(ordinalScores = FALSE), compare_encoding(ordinalScores = TRUE))# Time each model so the post can report relative run timesdfTimings <- tibble(model = character(), seconds = numeric())time_model <- function(model, expr) {t0 <- Sys.time()result <- force(expr)dfTimings <<- dfTimings %>% add_row(model = model, seconds = as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs")))result}# lm model (no hyperparameters, so fit_resamples instead of tune_grid)model_spec_lm <- get_model_spec(modelType = "lm")cv_results_lm <- time_model("lm",get_workflow(model_spec_lm) %>%fit_resamples(resamples = cv_folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse)) %>%collect_metrics() %>%select(mean_rmse = mean))# glmnet modelmodel_spec_glmnet <- get_model_spec(modelType = "glmnet")param_grid_glmnet <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "glmnet", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)cv_results_glmnet <- time_model("glmnet", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_glmnet, param_grid_glmnet))param_best_glmnet <- cv_results_glmnet %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)model_final_glmnet <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_glmnet, param_best_glmnet)# kernlab modelmodel_spec_kernlab <- get_model_spec(modelType = "kernlab")param_grid_kernlab <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "kernlab", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)cv_results_kernlab <- time_model("kernlab", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_kernlab, param_grid_kernlab))param_best_kernlab <- cv_results_kernlab %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)model_final_kernlab <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_kernlab, param_best_kernlab)# random forest model (ranger engine; objects keep the _rf names used in index.Rmd)model_spec_rf <- get_model_spec(modelType = "ranger")param_grid_rf <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "ranger", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)cv_results_rf <- time_model("ranger", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_rf, param_grid_rf))param_best_rf <- cv_results_rf %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)model_final_rf <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_rf, param_best_rf)# xgboost modelmodel_spec_xgboost <- get_model_spec(modelType = "xgboost")param_grid_xgboost <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "xgboost", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)cv_results_xgboost <- time_model("xgboost", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_xgboost, param_grid_xgboost))param_best_xgboost <- cv_results_xgboost %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)model_final_xgboost <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_xgboost, param_best_xgboost)plan(sequential)# the results that the post uses, which are saved to Ames_Tuning.RdavTuningResults <- c("model_spec_lm", "model_spec_glmnet", "model_spec_rf", "model_spec_xgboost", "model_spec_kernlab","model_final_glmnet", "model_final_rf", "model_final_xgboost", "model_final_kernlab", "cv_results_lm","cv_results_glmnet", "cv_results_rf", "cv_results_xgboost", "cv_results_kernlab", "param_grid_glmnet","param_grid_rf", "param_grid_xgboost", "param_grid_kernlab", "param_best_glmnet", "param_best_rf","param_best_xgboost", "param_best_kernlab", "dfTrain", "dfTest", "dfTrain_Proc","dfTest_Proc", "dfTimings", "get_preprocessing_recipe", "preprocessing_recipe", "vFeaturesCollinear","dfEncodingComparison", "cv_folds", "vFeaturesSkew")And this code decides whether to load the saved results or to run the tuning steps:
# The clean dataset from Part 1ames_data_file <- "../ames-housing-part1-eda/Ames_Housing_Clean.Rda"# Fingerprint (hash) of the inputs of the tuning: the data that it uses, and the code of the "tuning_steps"# chunk, which also sets the hyperparameter grids. Comments and spacing are removed from the code first, so# editing them does not start a new tuning run.envData <- new.env()load(ames_data_file, envir = envData)tuning_steps <- knitr::knit_code$get("tuning_steps")tuning_hash <- rlang::hash(list(data = list(envData$dfClean, envData$vTestIDs),code = deparse(parse(text = tuning_steps, keep.source = FALSE))))# If the saved results were made from the same inputs, load them. Otherwise, tune the models again and save# the new results together with the fingerprint of their inputs.envSaved <- new.env()if (file.exists("Ames_Tuning.Rda")) load("Ames_Tuning.Rda", envir = envSaved)if (identical(envSaved$tuning_hash, tuning_hash)) {list2env(as.list(envSaved), envir = environment())} else {eval(parse(text = tuning_steps))save(list = c(vTuningResults, "tuning_hash"), file = "Ames_Tuning.Rda")}rm(envData, envSaved)
summary:
In a previous post in this series, we explored the Ames Housing dataset.
In this post, we build linear and non-linear models, and we find out how well they predict the SalePrice of properties. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. A linear model adds up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that it learns from the data. A non-linear model can also learn curved relationships.

The categories of a nominal feature have no natural order. But if we sort the categories by their median SalePrice, we can find trends. To show the trends better, the SalePrice axis does not show the outliers. A box plot shows the middle half of the prices as a box, with a line at the median:
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist=map2(vFeaturesCat2,"SalePrice", ~ eda_plot_box(dfClean, .x, .y, yLimits = c(35000,410000))), ncol = 4)What’s notable?GarageType: buyers prefer built-in and attached garages to detached garages and other types.The categories of MSSubClass show that houses built in 1946 or later have higher prices than older houses.Multivariate Analysis: Three or More Features at a TimeIn this section, we look at how some related features change SalePrice together.
Numerical-Numerical-CategoricalTotalSF and GarageArea have some of the strongest correlations with SalePrice. Let’s see how these relationships change with NeighborhoodType and GarageType:
p1 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "TotalSF", "SalePrice", "NeighborhoodType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)p2 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "GarageArea", "SalePrice", "GarageType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)For the same total area, properties in some neighborhoods sell for more than in others.The properties without a garage form a separate group.For the same GarageArea, properties with built-in or attached garages usually sell for more.So NeighborhoodType and GarageType explain some of the differences in SalePrice.Categorical-Numerical-NumericalThe dots in the scatter plots overlap a lot. So let’s check these results in another way, and compare categories among properties of similar size. We split TotalSF and GarageArea into four groups (bins) with the same number of properties. Then we plot SalePrice for each category in each group. We also check whether central air conditioning (CentralAir) changes the price of properties of the same size:
p1 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))p2 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "GarageType", "SalePrice", "GarageArea", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))p3 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "CentralAir", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)# median SalePrice by category within each binget_bin_medians <- function(p) {p$data %>%group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), category = as.character(x)) %>%summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")}lBinMedians <- map(list(neighborhood = p1, garage = p2, air = p3), get_bin_medians)bin_median <- function(plotName, binNum, categoryName) {dfMedians <- lBinMedians[[plotName]]scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$category == categoryName], accuracy = 1)}What’s notable?The neighborhood is very important, even for properties of the same size. For the largest properties, the median SalePrice goes from $161,000 in Type5 neighborhoods to $327,000 in Type1 neighborhoods. Type1 neighborhoods have few or no properties in the smallest group, so the neighborhood and the size are also related.For the same GarageArea, built-in and attached garages go with higher prices than detached garages. For the largest garages, the median SalePrice is $299,018 for built-in garages, $253,000 for attached garages and $140,000 for detached garages. Some garage types have very few properties, so their box plots are less reliable.Properties with central air conditioning sell for more, at every size. For the largest properties, the median SalePrice is $262,140 with central air and $136,000 without it.Categorical-Categorical-NumericalDoes a combination of two categorical features tell us more about SalePrice? A heatmap answers this question. It is a grid of tiles, one tile for each combination of two categories:
p1 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "OverallQual", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")p2 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "GarageType", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")p3 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "MSSubClass", "MSZoning", "SalePrice")cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)# number of combinations, and those with fewer than 10 propertiesvCells <- map_int(list(p1, p2, p3), ~ nrow(.x$data))vSparse <- map_int(list(p1, p2, p3), ~ sum(.x$data$n < 10))Each tile shows the median SalePrice (by its color) and the number of properties. A tile is grey if it has fewer than 10 properties, because a median of so few properties is not reliable.
Some neighborhoods have more properties with a high OverallQual, so their prices are higher. But in Type4 neighborhoods, SalePrice clearly changes with the quality of the property.It is less clear whether GarageType has a large effect by itself. Buyers seem to prefer built-in and attached garages, but NeighborhoodType explains most of the differences.In both one-story and multi-story houses built after 1946, properties in low-density residential zones and floating village zones usually have higher prices.Many combinations are rare: 11 of the 34 combinations of OverallQual and NeighborhoodType, and 20 of the 46 combinations of MSSubClass and MSZoning, have fewer than 10 properties. So we can compare only the common combinations reliably. Also, a model would find it hard to learn how these features work together.# split the data back to training and testing sets# dfTrain <- dfClean %>% dplyr::slice(1:nrows_train)# dfTest <- dfClean %>% dplyr::slice(-(1:nrows_train))save(vFeaturesCat, vFeaturesNum, vFeaturesCor, dfClean, vTestIDs, file = "Ames_Housing_Clean.Rda")

Other posts in this series:Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data AnalysisDiamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear ModelsIn the previous posts, we found out which attributes of a diamond are important for its price. An exploratory data analysis showed that carat, clarity and color are the most important features to predict price. Then we built linear models to predict the prices, and we chose the best model by its metrics.
In this post, we use non-linear models to predict the prices of diamonds, and we compare them with the linear models. A non-linear model can learn curved relationships and interactions between features by itself.
Training Non-linear ModelsWe use three types of non-linear models:
randomForest builds many decision trees and takes the average of their predictions. A decision tree predicts a value by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as “Is carat more than 1?”.xgboost (gradient boosting) builds many small decision trees one after the other. Each new tree corrects some of the errors of the trees before it.keras builds a neural network. A neural network passes the features through layers of simple calculations, and it learns the strength of each connection from the data.We follow some of the same steps as for the linear models, and we change some features:
Split the dataset into a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%.Keep the same mix of clarity grades in both sets (stratified sampling).clarity, color and cut have ordered categories, from the lowest grade to the highest grade. randomForest can use these categories directly. But xgboost and keras need all the features as numbers. There are two methods to change categories into numbers:One-hot encoding: each category of clarity, color and cut becomes a new feature with the values 0 and 1. A disadvantage of this method is that the order of the grades is lost. But the training set is large, so the non-linear models can learn the order by themselves.Integer scores: the grades become the numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, from the lowest grade to the highest. But this method assumes that the steps between all the grades are equal, which may not be correct here.Center and scale all the values in the training set, so that all the features have similar ranges. Then put the features in a matrix (a table of numbers).Train a non-linear model on the training set.Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls the random split into the training set and the testing set.Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.Here are the average metrics for all the models that we trained with keras, randomForest and xgboost:
load("fit_models_keras.Rda")dfModels_keras <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "keras")best_model_results_keras <- best_model_resultsdfResults_keras <- best_model_results_keras$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "keras")load("fit_models_rf.Rda")dfModels_rf <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")best_model_results_rf <- best_model_resultsdfResults_rf <- best_model_results_rf$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")load("fit_models_xgb.Rda")dfModels_xgb <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")best_model_results_xgb <- best_model_resultsdfResults_xgb <- best_model_results_xgb$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")# combine the actual v/s predicted results from the best model using the 3 methodsdfResults <- map_df(list(dfResults_keras, dfResults_rf, dfResults_xgb), bind_rows) %>% select(type, everything()) %>% mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% group_by(type)# combine the average metrics from all the models using the 3 methodsdfModels <- map_df(list(dfModels_keras, dfModels_rf, dfModels_xgb), bind_rows) %>% select(type, everything()) %>% mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% gather(avg_metric, value, rmse, rsq, mae)# create an HTML tabledfModels %>% tidyHtmlTable(header = "type", cgroup1 = "avg_metric", cell_value = "value", rnames = "model", align = "|rrr|rrr|rrr")kerasrandomForestxgboostprice ~ .c(“989.71”, “0.93”, “360.55”)c(“529.28”, “0.98”, “262.35”)c(“540.76”, “0.98”, “280.49”)price ~ caratc(“1499.2”, “0.86”, “860.29”)c(“1427.25”, “0.87”, “816.1”)c(“1427.35”, “0.87”, “815.76”)price ~ carat + clarityc(“1040.69”, “0.93”, “590.32”)c(“1006.61”, “0.94”, “548.67”)c(“992.46”, “0.94”, “544.48”)price ~ carat + clarity + colorc(“645.4”, “0.97”, “358.85”)c(“571.73”, “0.98”, “305.17”)c(“575.3”, “0.98”, “306.86”)price ~ carat + clarity + color + cutc(“626.78”, “0.98”, “347.99”)c(“545.02”, “0.98”, “285.96”)c(“541.63”, “0.98”, “282.38”)The R-squared values (rsq) show that all the models learn the complex relationship between price and carat very well. For the linear models, we had to change both price and carat to a log scale. The neural network and the decision tree models learn this relationship by themselves. The root mean squared error (RMSE) is in dollars, so it is easy to understand. The average price of a diamond is about $4000, and the prices vary by about $4000 (the standard deviation). So the RMSE values of the models are very low. With carat, clarity and color, the RMSE is between $572 and $645. The best linear model with the same features has an RMSE of about $816.
The exploratory data analysis helps here, because the models with only carat, clarity and color give excellent results. If we add cut, the RMSE goes down only a little.
Even the base models with all the features (price ~ .) explain the variation in the prices very well, although some of their features repeat the same information. Decision trees and neural networks are not affected by such repeated information (multicollinearity) as much as linear models are. To find the most important features of these models, we can explain their predictions one at a time.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic ExplanationsLIME is a method to explain the predictions of a “black box” model, which is a model whose calculations are too complex for a person to follow. LIME explains one prediction at a time. It assumes that, close to a single diamond, the complex model behaves like a simple linear model. So LIME fits a simple model around that one diamond. The simple model then explains how the complex model makes its prediction for that diamond.
LIME uses these steps:
Take one diamond, and make many copies of it with small random changes to its features.Measure how similar each copy is to the original diamond.Use the complex model to predict the price of each copy.Choose a small number (m) of features that best explain the predicted prices.Fit a simple model to the copies, with the m features. Give more weight to the copies that are more similar to the original diamond.Use the weights of the simple model to explain the prediction for the original diamond.Here, we choose the 5 features that best explain the predictions for 6 random diamonds from the testing set.
# Plot Feature Importance by sampleplot_features(explanation_keras, ncol = 3) + labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from a keras model",subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +theme_quant() +theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))plot_features(explanation_xgb, ncol = 3) + labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from an xgboost model",subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +theme_quant() +theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))For these 6 random diamonds, the most important features for the predictions are carat, clarity, color, x and y.
# Plot Feature Importance Heatmapplot_explanations(explanation_keras) +labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from a keras model",subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +theme_quant() +theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))plot_explanations(explanation_xgb) +labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from an xgboost model",subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +theme_quant() +theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))We know that x and y have a very strong correlation with carat, so they repeat the same information. That is why it is good practice to remove such repeated features before we train a model. For keras, the model with carat, clarity and color has the best metrics. For the decision tree models, the model with all the features is a little more accurate, but it needs many more features.
Actual v/s PredictedFinally, here are the scatter plots of the actual prices against the predicted prices, for the best model of each type on the testing set:
p1 <- dfResults %>%ungroup() %>%rename(price = actual) %>%eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0,labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(linear scale)")) +theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))p2 <- dfResults %>%ungroup() %>%rename(price = actual) %>%eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(log scale)")) +theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)The scatter plots use both normal (linear) axes and log axes. The R-squared and RMSE values of the 3 methods are similar. But for expensive diamonds, the predictions of keras are more spread out than the predictions of the two decision tree methods. For cheap diamonds, the decision tree methods seem to predict the prices better, with less spread.
As with the linear models, the spread of the predicted prices increases with price. The decision tree methods keep their predictions close to the range of prices in the data. Their highest predictions are $18,340 (randomForest) and $19,118 (xgboost). The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,823. A randomForest prediction is an average of prices from the training data, so it cannot be higher than those prices. xgboost adds up many small corrections, so its predictions can be only a little higher. A neural network, like a linear model, can predict prices far above the prices in the data (extrapolation). The highest price that keras predicts is $26,591. So the non-linear methods learn the relationships between price and the other features very well, and the decision tree methods also keep their predictions within a reasonable range.
SummaryAll 3 non-linear methods learn the complex relationship between price, carat and the other features by themselves. They do not need feature engineering.The exploratory data analysis helps us remove repeated features before we train the models. This makes the training faster. For keras, it also gives much better metrics.keras neural networks train the fastest, because they can use a GPU (a graphics processor that does many calculations at the same time).Of the two decision tree methods, xgboost trains much faster than randomForest.randomForest and xgboost can use several CPU cores at the same time. On a local computer, the amount of memory (RAM) is the only limit.

In a previous post in this series, we explored the diamonds dataset. We found that price has a strong correlation with carat, x, y and z, and that log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). For diamonds of similar weight, clarity and color also seemed to help predict the price.
In this post, we build linear models and find out how well they predict the price of diamonds. A linear model predicts a value by adding up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that the model learns from the data.
First, let’s build a simple base model that uses all the features, without any changes to them. Its results give us a starting point to compare with:
model_lm <- lm(price ~ ., data = diamonds)summary(model_lm)Call:lm(formula = price ~ ., data = diamonds)Residuals:Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -21376 -592 -183 376 10694 Coefficients:Estimate Std.
