The model summary shows that this model is overfitted. An overfitted model learns the noise in the data, not only the true patterns, so it does not work well on new data. For example, we know that depth and table have no effect on price, but the model says that they are very important.
The table above also shows the root mean squared error (RMSE) and other metrics. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, in the same units as the price. A lower RMSE means better predictions.
Let’s plot the actual prices against the predicted prices, to see how well this base model works.
augment(model_lm, diamonds) %>%eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", ".fitted", nLabel = 0, labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted price from a base linear model")If the predictions are good, the points are close to the dashed line at 45 degrees, where the predicted price is equal to the actual price. This base model predicts the prices badly. Worst of all, it predicts negative prices for cheap diamonds. To prevent such impossible results, we must use log(price) instead of price.
Feature EngineeringFeature engineering means that we create new features from the existing features, to make the patterns easier for a model to learn.
We know that the price of a diamond has a strong correlation with its size. If all other things are equal, a larger diamond has a higher price.
As a first estimate, we can treat a diamond as a box with the dimensions x, y and z. Then its volume is x * y * z.These 3 dimensions have a strong correlation with each other. So we can calculate one average dimension as the cube root of volume. This average dimension keeps a straight-line relationship with log(price).
We can also calculate an average dimension with high school chemistry. Mass, volume and density are related by this equation:
$ density = mass/volume $
1 carat is 0.2 grams. If we divide the mass by the density of diamond (3.51 grams per cubic centimeter), we get the volume. The cube root of the volume gives an average dimension.
dfInput <- diamonds %>%mutate(row = row_number(),volume = x*y*z,`average dimension` = volume ^ (1/3),volume2 = carat * 0.2/3.51,`average dimension2` = (volume2 ^ (1/3)) * 10) # Multiply by 10 to convert from cm to mmeda_plot_scatter(dfInput, c("average dimension", "average dimension2"), "price", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar,nLabel = 3, feature_id = "row", labelBy = "leverage") +labs(title = "Scatterplot of price v/s average dimension")# the point with the most leverage on the linear fit of price on the dimension-based featuredfLeverage <- dfInput %>%mutate(leverage = hatvalues(lm(price ~ `average dimension`, data = dfInput))) %>%slice_max(leverage, n = 1)The two methods give similar results, but the density method gives a narrower range. Which method is more reliable?In each panel, the labels show the row numbers of the diamonds with the most leverage. Leverage tells how much a point can pull the straight line towards itself. Points that are far from the others along the x axis have the most leverage.With the dimensions, the most extreme point is the diamond in row 24068. It is a 2 carat diamond with a recorded width y of 58.9 mm. This value is clearly a recording error. The other labelled points are diamonds with an average dimension of 0. With the density method, the labelled points are simply the largest diamonds in the dataset.Also, 20 values of z are 0. In 7 of these diamonds, x and y are also 0. So these dimensions were not recorded correctly.
diamonds %>% dplyr::filter(x == 0 | y == 0 | z == 0)# A tibble: 20 × 10carat cut color clarity depth table price x y z<dbl> <ord> <ord> <ord> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>1 1 Premium G SI2 59.1 59 3142 6.55 6.48 02 1.01 Premium H I1 58.1 59 3167 6.66 6.6 03 1.1 Premium G SI2 63 59 3696 6.5 6.47 04 1.01 Premium F SI2 59.2 58 3837 6.5 6.47 05 1.5 Good G I1 64 61 4731 7.15 7.04 06 1.07 Ideal F SI2 61.6 56 4954 0 6.62 07 1 Very Good H VS2 63.3 53 5139 0 0 08 1.15 Ideal G VS2 59.2 56 5564 6.88 6.83 09 1.14 Fair G VS1 57.5 67 6381 0 0 010 2.18 Premium H SI2 59.4 61 12631 8.49 8.45 011 1.56 Ideal G VS2 62.2 54 12800 0 0 012 2.25 Premium I SI1 61.3 58 15397 8.52 8.42 013 1.2 Premium D VVS1 62.1 59 15686 0 0 014 2.2 Premium H SI1 61.2 59 17265 8.42 8.37 015 2.25 Premium H SI2 62.8 59 18034 0 0 016 2.02 Premium H VS2 62.7 53 18207 8.02 7.95 017 2.8 Good G SI2 63.8 58 18788 8.9 8.85 018 0.71 Good F SI2 64.1 60 2130 0 0 019 0.71 Good F SI2 64.1 60 2130 0 0 020 1.12 Premium G I1 60.4 59 2383 6.71 6.67 0For all of these diamonds, the carat values are correct. So carat is probably more accurate than the dimensions,and we prefer the density method to create this feature.
Also, the density is a constant. So we do not need to divide by it to calculate the volume. Instead, we can take the cube root of carat itself. Then we expect a straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(carat^{1/3}\).A straight-line relationship is what a linear model needs, because the model adds up its features in a straight-line way.
The geometry suggests a cube root. But does the cube root give the best straight line? Let’s compare it with other transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points of log(price):
p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(diamonds, "carat", "price")p_transforms# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panelsvR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%pull(r_squared) %>%set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))The cube root (R-squared 0.924) is much better than carat without a transform (0.847). But log(carat) is even better (0.933). A straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(log(carat)\) is easy to understand: the coefficient of \(log(carat)\) is the percentage change in price when carat increases by 1%. We will try both transforms in our models.
Training Linear ModelsThese are the steps to build the linear models and measure how well they work:
Split the dataset into two sets: a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%. The model learns from the training set. Then we check its predictions on the testing set, which has diamonds that the model has not seen.clarity is one of the most important features. So we split the data in a way that keeps the same mix of clarity grades in both sets. This is called stratified sampling.Train (fit) a linear model on the training set.Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls which diamonds go into each set. With different seeds, we get different random splits, so one lucky or unlucky split does not decide the results.Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.Here is one split into a training set and a testing set, stratified by clarity. Both sets have a similar mix of clarity grades.
set.seed(1333)train_split <- diamonds %>% select(price, everything()) %>% initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")dfTrain <- training(train_split)dfTest <- testing(train_split)Hmisc::describe(dfTrain$clarity)dfTrain$clarity n missing distinct 40453 0 8 Value I1 SI2 SI1 VS2 VS1 VVS2 VVS1 IFFrequency 557 6904 9810 9197 6109 3785 2766 1325Proportion 0.014 0.171 0.243 0.227 0.151 0.094 0.068 0.033Hmisc::describe(dfTest$clarity)dfTest$clarity n missing distinct 13487 0 8 Value I1 SI2 SI1 VS2 VS1 VVS2 VVS1 IFFrequency 184 2290 3255 3061 2062 1281 889 465Proportion 0.014 0.170 0.241 0.227 0.153 0.095 0.066 0.034We ran each model 5 times with different seeds. Here are the average metrics. R-squared (rsq) tells how much of the variation in price the model explains, and the mean absolute error (mae) is the average size of a prediction error:
fit_linear_model <- function(randomSeed, model_formula, get_model = FALSE) {set.seed(randomSeed)train_split <- diamonds %>% select(price, everything()) %>% initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")dfTrain <- training(train_split)dfTest <- testing(train_split)# fit a linear modelmodel_lm <- lm(model_formula, data = dfTrain)# predict on testing set to determine rmse predict_lm <- predict(model_lm, dfTest)# predict on testing set with outliersdfResults <- dfTest %>% mutate(actual = price) %>% mutate(estimate = predict_lm %>% exp()) %>% select(actual, estimate)if(get_model) {return(list(model_lm, dfResults))} else {return(dfResults)}}set.seed(1000)vRandomSeeds <- sample(9999, 5)dfModels <- expand_grid(seed = vRandomSeeds, model = c("log(price) ~ .","log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3))","log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity","log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color","log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color + cut","log(price) ~ log(carat)","log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity","log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color","log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color + cut")) %>%mutate(results = map2(seed, model, ~ fit_linear_model(.x, as.formula(.y)))) %>% mutate(metrics = map(results, ~ metrics(.x, truth = actual, estimate = estimate))) %>%select(-results) %>% unnest(cols = metrics) %>% select(-.estimator) %>% spread(.metric, .estimate) %>% group_by(model) %>% summarise_at(vars(rmse, rsq, mae), mean)dfModels# A tibble: 9 × 4model rmse rsq mae<chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>1 log(price) ~ . 12085. 0.756 559.2 log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) 2525. 0.741 1023.3 log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity 2173. 0.827 871.4 log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color 1725. 0.888 624.5 log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color + cut 1718. 0.891 618.6 log(price) ~ log(carat) 1624. 0.839 840.7 log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity 1225. 0.910 637.8 log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color 816. 0.959 418.9 log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color + cut 795. 0.961 402.# average metric of a modelmodel_metric <- function(model_formula, metric) dfModels[[metric]][dfModels$model == model_formula]The first model, with all the features, is overfitted.
Each model with log(carat) is much better than the same model with the cube root of carat. With clarity and color, the RMSE goes down from $1,725 to $816, and the R-squared goes up from 0.888 to 0.959.
The model with log(carat), clarity and color gives the best combination of a low RMSE and a high R-squared, so it explains the most variation.This is our final model.If we add cut, the RMSE goes down only a little, to $795. So we do not use cut, and we keep the model simpler.
Here is the summary of our final model:
formula_string <- "log(price) ~ log(carat) + clarity + color"fit_lm <- fit_linear_model(1333, as.formula(formula_string), get_model = T)# the cube root model on the same split, for comparisonfit_lm_cuberoot <- fit_linear_model(1333, as.formula("log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3)) + clarity + color"), get_model = T)summary(fit_lm[[1]])Call:lm(formula = model_formula, data = dfTrain)Residuals:Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -0.9796 -0.0898 -0.0003 0.0876 1.4300 Coefficients:Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 8.48644 0.00122 6935.93 < 0.0000000000000002 ***log(carat) 1.87823 0.00134 1403.69 < 0.0000000000000002 ***clarity.L 0.95166 0.00420 226.70 < 0.0000000000000002 ***clarity.Q -0.26263 0.00393 -66.75 < 0.0000000000000002 ***clarity.C 0.14657 0.00338 43.37 < 0.0000000000000002 ***clarity^4 -0.07520 0.00271 -27.78 < 0.0000000000000002 ***clarity^5 0.03126 0.00222 14.11 < 0.0000000000000002 ***clarity^6 -0.00520 0.00193 -2.69 0.0071 ** clarity^7 0.03623 0.00171 21.22 < 0.0000000000000002 ***color.L -0.43986 0.00242 -181.61 < 0.0000000000000002 ***color.Q -0.09854 0.00222 -44.32 < 0.0000000000000002 ***color.C -0.01673 0.00208 -8.05 0.00000000000000086 ***color^4 0.01116 0.00191 5.85 0.00000000508834206 ***color^5 -0.00155 0.00180 -0.86 0.3884 color^6 0.00175 0.00164 1.07 0.2869 ---Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1Residual standard error: 0.138 on 40438 degrees of freedomMultiple R-squared: 0.982,	Adjusted R-squared: 0.982 F-statistic: 1.53e+05 on 14 and 40438 DF, p-value: <0.0000000000000002A residual is the difference between the actual value and the predicted value, here of log(price). Residual plots show if the errors of a model have a pattern. If the model is good, the residuals look like random noise around 0. Here are the four standard residual plots of our final model:
# labels are off: the row numbers of a random training set do not identify the diamondseda_plot_residuals(fit_lm[[1]], nLabel = 0)vStdResid <- rstandard(fit_lm[[1]])vCooks <- cooks.distance(fit_lm[[1]])Residuals vs Fitted: The residuals stay close to 0 for all predicted values, and the red smooth line is almost flat. So the model captures the relationship well. The small curve shows that a little non-linearity remains. At the highest predicted values, the residuals form a sloping edge below 0. The reason is that no diamond in the data costs more than $18,823, so for the largest predictions, the actual price can only be lower.Normal Q-Q: In the middle, the points follow the dashed line, so most residuals are normally distributed. But the tails, especially the upper tail, are longer: some diamonds cost much more than the model predicts. 160 of the 40453 diamonds in the training set have a standardized residual larger than 3, or smaller than -3.Scale-Location: The smooth line is almost flat, so the spread of the errors is about the same for cheap and expensive diamonds. The log of price makes the spread stable. Without it, the errors grow with the price.Residuals vs Leverage: No diamond has a high leverage. The largest Cook’s distance is only 0.0067. A point needs a Cook’s distance of about 0.5 or more to pull the model strongly, so the plot does not even reach the dashed contours that mark 0.5 and 1. No single diamond controls the model.If clarity and color do not change, a 1% increase in carat increases the predicted price by about 1.88%.
Here is a scatter plot of the actual prices against the prices that our final model predicts for the testing set:
fit_lm[[2]] %>%rename(price = actual) %>%eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +labs(title = bquote(log(price) == log(carat) + clarity + color))The points are close to the 45-degree line. But at the high end, the differences between the actual and predicted prices become larger.The predictions of the final model are also much less extreme. The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,804. The highest predicted price is $28,130. But the cube root model predicts prices as high as $59,082 for the same testing set. Like all linear models, the final model can still predict prices above the highest prices in the data (this is called extrapolation).

In a previous post in this series, we explored the diamonds dataset. We found that price has a strong correlation with carat, x, y and z, and that log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). For diamonds of similar weight, clarity and color also seemed to help predict the price.
In this post, we build linear models and find out how well they predict the price of diamonds. A linear model predicts a value by adding up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that the model learns from the data.

In this case study, we explore the diamonds dataset. Then, in the next posts, we build models that predict the price of a diamond. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. Some models are linear (they use straight-line relationships) and some are non-linear (they can also learn curves).
Data DescriptionThe diamonds dataset has almost 54,000 diamonds. For each diamond, it gives the price (in US dollars of 2008) and other attributes, such as the weight and the quality grades. We call each attribute a feature.
dfDescription <- tribble(~ Attribute, ~ Description,"price", "price in 2008 USD","carat", "weight of a diamond (1 carat = 0.2 gms)","cut", "quality of the cut (Fair, Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal)","color", "diamond color from D (best) to J (worst)","clarity", "a measurement of how clear the diamond is (I1 (worst), SI2, SI1, VS2, VS1, VVS2, VVS1, IF (best))","x", "length in mm","y", "width in mm","z", "depth in mm","depth", "total depth percentage = z/mean(x, y)","table", "width of the top of diamond relative to widest point")knitr::kable(dfDescription)AttributeDescriptionpriceprice in 2008 USDcaratweight of a diamond (1 carat = 0.2 gms)cutquality of the cut (Fair, Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal)colordiamond color from D (best) to J (worst)claritya measurement of how clear the diamond is (I1 (worst), SI2, SI1, VS2, VS1, VVS2, VVS1, IF (best))xlength in mmywidth in mmzdepth in mmdepthtotal depth percentage = z/mean(x, y)tablewidth of the top of diamond relative to widest pointData SummariesvFeaturesCat <- dfInput %>% select_if(is.factor) %>% colnames() vFeaturesNum <- dfInput %>% select_if(is.numeric) %>% colnames()visdat::vis_dat(dfInput) + theme_quant()This chart shows all the features and their types. No values are missing in this dataset.
Next, we look at the numbers for each feature:

diamond is about USD 4000. Many diamonds are much more expensive than most others. We call such unusual values outliers.carat: The average weight is about 0.8 carat. About 75% of the diamonds weigh less than 1 carat. The 5 largest values show that there are many outliers at the high end.cut: About 40% of the diamonds have an Ideal cut. Only 3% have a Fair cut. So the categories are not balanced: some categories have many more diamonds than others.color: Most diamonds have a color grade from E to H. Fewer diamonds have the color grade J.clarity: Most diamonds have a clarity grade from SI2 to VS1. About 1% have the worst grade, I1. Only about 3% have the best grade, IF.depth: Most depth values are between 60 and 64. There are outliers at both the low end and the high end.table: Most table values are between 54 and 65. There are outliers at both ends.x: The length of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 4 and 8. Some values are 0, which means that nobody recorded them.y: The width of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 3.5 and 8. 7 values are 0.z: The depth of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 2.5 and 8.5. 20 values are 0.Univariate Analysis: One Feature at a TimeIn this section, we look at each feature by itself.
Numerical Featureseda_plot_histograms(dfInput, vFeaturesNum)The plots show outliers in each feature. Let’s remove the outliers and plot the features again. We use a common rule: a value is an outlier if it is more than 2.5 interquartile ranges from the median. The median is the middle value: half the values are below it and half are above it. The interquartile range is the width of the middle half of the values. The outliers themselves have almost no effect on these two numbers, so the rule is reliable. A rule that uses the average would be less reliable, because the outliers pull the average towards them.
makeOutliersNA <- function(Z) {# values more than 2.5 interquartile ranges from the median become NAifelse(flag_outliers(Z, nIQR = 2.5), NA, Z)}# convert outliers to NA valuesdfInput <- dfInput %>% mutate_at(vFeaturesNum, makeOutliersNA)eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, vFeaturesNum) + labs(title = "Histograms of numerical features excluding outliers")Without the outliers, the ranges of the values are more reasonable. carat and price are right skewed: most values are small, and a few values are much larger.
Let’s plot price on a log scale. On a log scale, each step on the axis multiplies the value by the same amount (for example, from $100 to $1,000 to $10,000). This makes it easier to see the spread of skewed values:
eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, "price", nBins = 100, xLog = T, xLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))The plot has two peaks. This means that two price ranges are the most common: one just below USD 1000 and one near USD 5000. Interestingly, almost no diamonds cost about USD 1500. So the plot shows a big gap at that price.
Categorical Featurescowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_column(dfInput, .x)), ncol = 2)The plots clearly show that the categories of cut and clarity are not balanced.
Bivariate Analysis: Two Features at a TimeIn this section, we look at how price changes with each of the other features.
Numerical-numericalFirst, we measure the correlation of price with each numerical feature. A correlation is a number from -1 to 1. It tells how closely two features move together in a straight line. A value near 1 means that when one feature goes up, the other also goes up. A value near -1 means that the other goes down. A value near 0 means that there is no straight-line relationship.
eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfInput[vFeaturesNum] %>% drop_na(), outlineVar = "price", plotTitle = "Clustered correlations of numerical features")price has a very strong correlation with carat and with the dimensions x, y and z. These four features are also strongly correlated with each other, because they all measure the size of a diamond. So a linear model cannot easily separate their effects. table and depth have almost no correlation with price. So they are not useful to predict the price.
Now let’s look at the scatter plots. A scatter plot shows one dot for each diamond:
eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))Without the outliers, price grows faster and faster as carat, x, y and z increase. So let’s plot price on a log scale:
eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLog = T, yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))On a log scale, log(price) has an approximately straight-line (linear) relationship with x, y and z. But its relationship with carat is still curved. Also, the spread (variance) of price increases as the diamonds get larger.
Can we change carat with a simple formula so that its relationship with log(price) becomes a straight line? We call such a change a transform. Let’s compare some common transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points. R-squared is a number from 0 to 1. It tells how much of the variation in log(price) the straight line explains. A higher value means that the line fits the points better:
p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(dfInput, "carat", "price")p_transforms# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panelsvR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%pull(r_squared) %>%set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))log(carat) gives the best straight-line fit, with an R-squared of 0.926. The cube root is second (0.919) and the square root is third (0.91). carat without a transform has the lowest R-squared, 0.862. So log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). This means that when the weight increases by a given percentage, the price increases by an approximately constant percentage. We will use this result when we create features for the models (Feature Engineering).
Numerical-CategoricalLet’s look at price for each category of the categorical features. A box plot shows the middle half of the prices as a box, with a line at the median:
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_box(dfInput, .x, "price", yLimits = c(300, 8000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))), ncol = 3)To show the trends better, the price axis of these box plots does not show the most expensive diamonds. The box plots are surprising: for cut, color and clarity, the median price usually goes down as the grade gets better. This is very strange. We will find the reason in the multivariate analysis.
The median price goes down steadily from a Fair cut to an Ideal cut.For color, the median price goes down from J (worst) to G (middle grade). Then it goes up, and it goes down again for D (best).For clarity, the median price goes up from I1 to SI2. Then it goes down steadily to IF.Multivariate Analysis: Three or More Features at a TimeSo far, we know that carat, x, y and z have the strongest relationship with price. The grades of cut, color and clarity also seem to have some effect on the median price. Let’s use scatter plots to look at these relationships together:
Numerical-Numerical-Categoricalcowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, "carat", "price", .x, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), ncol = 2)The dots overlap a lot. But for diamonds of the same carat weight, price clearly goes up as clarity gets better. color shows the same pattern, but it is weaker. cut does not show any effect.
So, for diamonds of the same weight, both color and clarity explain some of the differences in price.
All FeaturesWhy do the diamonds with better grades seem cheaper in the bivariate analysis? To find out, we measure the association between every pair of features. An association tells how strongly two features are related. Here, we rank the grades of cut, color and clarity from worst to best. Then we can compare them with the numerical features with Spearman’s rank correlation. This correlation uses the ranks of the values instead of the values themselves, so it also works for grades:
eda_plot_association_matrix(dfInput, method = "spearman", ordinalAsNumeric = T, outlineVar = "price",plotTitle = "Spearman correlations, with grades ranked from worst to best")mAssoc <- association_matrix(dfInput, method = "spearman", ordinalAsNumeric = T)carat has a negative correlation with clarity (-0.37) and with color (-0.24). This means that diamonds with better grades are usually smaller.price has a very strong correlation with carat (0.96). So price also has a negative correlation with clarity (-0.21) and with color (-0.13).carat, x, y and z form a tight group, and they are almost perfectly correlated with each other. So, to predict the price, these features give almost the same information.Categorical-Numerical-NumericalIn the scatter plots, the dots overlap too much to show how much each grade matters. So let’s compare grades among diamonds of similar weight. We split the diamonds into four groups (bins) of equal size by carat. Then we plot price for each grade in each group:
lBinPlots <- map(c("clarity", "color", "cut"), ~ eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfInput, .x, "price", "carat", yLog = T,yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)))cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = lBinPlots, ncol = 1)# median price by grade within each carat binget_bin_medians <- function(p) {p$data %>%group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), grade = as.character(x)) %>%summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")}dfBinMedians_clarity <- get_bin_medians(lBinPlots[[1]])bin_median <- function(dfMedians, binNum, gradeName) {scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$grade == gradeName], accuracy = 1)}# median carat by claritydfCarat_clarity <- dfInput %>% group_by(clarity) %>% summarise(carat = median(carat, na.rm = T))These plots explain the strange box plots of the bivariate analysis:
In each carat group, the median price usually goes up as clarity gets better. The effect is clearest for the heaviest diamonds: the median price goes from $3,985 for I1 to $10,332 for IF. The prices of the best grades (VVS2 to IF) are close to each other, and they are not always in order.In each group, price also goes up as color gets better from J to G. But the best grades (G to D) have about the same price. For the heaviest diamonds, D and E are even a little cheaper than G.cut does not show a clear trend, even for diamonds of similar weight.Diamonds with better grades seem cheaper overall because they are usually smaller. The median weight of an I1 diamond is 1.07 carat. The median weight of an IF diamond is only 0.35 carat. So carat is a confounder: it is related to both price and the grades, and it hides the true effect of the grades. To measure the effect of clarity or color, we must compare diamonds of similar weight.
Next, let’s check whether table and depth affect price together with color and clarity:
dfFeatures <- expand_grid(feat1 = c("depth","table"), feat2 = c("color","clarity")) %>% arrange(desc(feat2))cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map2(dfFeatures$feat1, dfFeatures$feat2, ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, .x, "price", .y, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), nrow = 2)These plots do not show any pattern. So table and depth do not help to predict price.
Categorical-Categorical-NumericalDoes clarity together with cut or color tell us more about price? A heatmap answers this question. It shows a grid of tiles, one for each combination of two categories. The color of each tile shows the median price of the diamonds in that combination:
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(c("cut","color"), ~ eda_plot_heatmap(dfInput, .x, "clarity", "price")), nrow = 2)The second heatmap is more interesting. From the bottom left to the top right, the grades of color and clarity get better, and the median price usually goes down. Again, this is the opposite of what we expect, because the diamonds with the best color and clarity should be the most expensive. As we saw above, the reason is that diamonds with better grades are usually smaller.
For cut and clarity, the median prices do not show a clear pattern. Each tile shows its number of diamonds. One combination (Fair cut and IF clarity) has fewer than 10 diamonds. Its tile is grey, because a median of so few diamonds is not reliable.
SummaryHere is what we found in this exploratory data analysis (EDA), which is the first study of a dataset before we build models:
price is right skewed. On a log scale, it has two peaks, so diamonds are popular in two different price ranges.carat: about 75% of the diamonds weigh less than 1 carat. The spread of prices increases with weight. log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat).cut is not balanced: about 40% of the diamonds have an Ideal cut.color is not balanced: only about 5% of the diamonds have the color grade J.clarity is not balanced at the two ends: only 1.5% of the diamonds have the grade I1, and only 3.3% have the grade IF.price has a strong correlation with carat and with the dimensions x, y and z. table and depth have almost no correlation with price.For diamonds of the same weight, clarity and color explain some of the differences in price. Overall, better grades seem to lower the price only because diamonds with better grades are usually smaller. cut has little effect.save(vFeaturesCat, vFeaturesNum, makeOutliersNA, file = "diamondClean.Rda")

It is important to understand the building blocks of systematic investing strategies before learning how to build them. Here is a schematic from the book, Inside the Black Box - The Simple Truth about Quantitative Trading by Rishi Narang, that provides a good way to visualize these building blocks and how they fit together in a system.
The Black Box Revealed
The author had aptly titled it - The Black Box Revealed, since that is how most people perceive it to be from the outside. From this schematic, it is easier to understand and visualize how a system is built with a systematic approach.
Here are the components of the system:
Data - Encapsulates the processes of raw data collection, cleaning and preparation in tidy form to be used by the models.Alpha Model - Describes the core strategy, product universe (stocks, ETFs, futures) and the rules to be implemented.Risk Model - Describes position sizes or how capital/risk is allocated. This is just as much important as the alpha model itself.Transaction Cost Model - Describes the transaction costs by product. These may be theoretical numbers while backtesting the strategy using historical data and later adjusted based on live execution data.Portfolio Construction Model - Describes how a portfolio is constructed after putting together positions by product across one or more rules of the core strategy.Execution Model - Encapsulates a live trading system. Describes the tactical implementation of the core strategy.Research - Sound research forms the underpinning of all models and is driven by quantitative and statistical analysis.The interactions shown are typical, although there could be more depending upon the implementation. More than one model could also be combined together, depending upon how the strategy is formulated. Nonetheless, for most practitioners looking to build a complete system from scratch, this is a pretty good blueprint.
